chunks.text:
TITLE: Figma variables v1 caused more harm than help at scale
TAGS: designsystems, pwc, figma
TYPE: project | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-07-17 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

When Figma shipped variables in 2023, it was the feature we'd needed for years: our system had to support multiple color themes, and mode switching was the answer. Another designer on the design system team and I rebuilt the entire library on variables. Then we published it to 120-plus designers and hundreds and hundreds of connected Figma files, and it turned into months of chaos.

## What went wrong

Files ended up with a mix of styles and variables, which was survivable: select everything, use selection colors, swap to variables. But something got corrupted in one of our merges and duplicate instances of the variables and tokens appeared in consuming files. We spent a stressful few months troubleshooting people's files and helping them revert, and in some cases even Figma support couldn't fix it. The best theory anyone landed on was cache versioning, some stale snapshot of the library file. Nobody ever truly fixed it.

The lesson: a v1 platform feature, even one you genuinely need, is not mature enough to bet a live library on. At that scale the blast radius is every file downstream. The library in question is the one from I ran the design system serving 3000 products at PwC, and the thing variables eventually delivered anyway is why Design tokens are the unlock. Hub: Design Systems MOC.

TITLE: I rebuilt PwC's design system in Figma to prove the switch
TAGS: designsystems, pwc, figma
TYPE: project | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-07-17 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

In early 2022 PwC was still running on Sketch, Abstract, and InVision. Fresh off the reusable-components approach from my agency years, I proposed doing the same thing in Figma, and then I proved it the hard way: I led rebuilding the entire design system, the fourth iteration at the time, in Figma, taking on 80-plus percent of the work myself. Months of it happened in my free time on top of actual product work.

It was very manual. Figma could import Sketch files, but layers, components, and styling all needed rework. Funny detail: tokens didn't even exist in Figma yet, you only had styles and themes you could publish in a library. The fourth version was more robust, with multiple color themes, so a clean-cut rebuild in Figma made far more sense than dragging it forward in Sketch.

The rebuild was good enough to demo how much faster Figma was, even just throwing things together in a shared canvas. That demo convinced leadership to invest, and we ran a trial with a few pilot projects. The department-wide rollout that followed is its own story: I pitched and led PwC's migration to Figma, and what it taught me about adoption is Rolling out a design system is a teaching job. Hub: Design Systems MOC.

A digital garden is more of a philosophy than a website. It's a mindset for how you approach work, in whatever craft you're in. It lowers the barrier to sharing something publicly while also holding you accountable to closing threads. As a neurodivergent, it's really helpful to let your brain go wherever it wants and follow what catches your eye. chunks.title: A todo app should be easy to capture unopinionated and clear your mind
chunks.text:
TITLE: A todo app should be easy to capture unopinionated and clear your mind
TAGS: productivity, tools, opinions
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2024-09-13 | UPDATED: 2026-07-26

I judge every todo app on three things, in this order: it has to be easy to capture into, it has to be unopinionated, and it has to actually clear your mind. Everything else is decoration.

Easy to capture means I can get a task in from my phone or my desk without thinking about where it goes, at whatever level of detail I happen to have. Sometimes that's four words, sometimes it's a full breakdown with notes. If capture has friction, the app is already dead, because the tasks just never make it in.

Unopinionated means the app doesn't force its methodology on me. A lot of productivity tools are really someone else's system with a UI on top, and the moment my week doesn't match their model I'm fighting the tool. And clearing your mind is the whole point: the reason to write it down is to stop carrying it, so if I still feel the weight of my list after using the app, it failed at the only job that matters.

Picking a todo app is like picking a car. You want something reliable to get you from A to B, and all the bells and whistles are irrelevant if your actual usage is light. This is only about personal productivity; team work happens in whatever the team uses, Asana, Notion, Trello, or Todoist. What I landed on is Things 3 is the todo app I settled on, and the wider tool stack is at Figma and Bear are my daily tools. Full write-up at /#writing/the-search-for-the-best-todo-app. Hubs: PKM MOC, Site MOC.

The lesson running through my whole design systems career is that tokens are the unlock. They're what make multiple themes manageable, they're what we were missing for years before Figma shipped variables, and they're the layer that lets a small team control a big system, which is why Most companies do not need a custom design system.

There's an AI angle now too. In current workflows, agents consume design through the context around it, and design tokens are that context. If you build on a popular base like Material, shadcn/ui, or Tailwind, you get to leverage all the public material and training those agents already have about it. Implement something fully bespoke and the agents know nothing. That's the same accelerator logic as AI amplifies your process it does not fix it: the leverage goes to whoever structures their system so the tools can use it.

Getting there the hard way is documented in Figma variables v1 caused more harm than help at scale. Hub: Design Systems MOC.

CREATED: 2025-05-24 | UPDATED: 2026-07-26

Everything I write lives in plain markdown files because of file over app: the notes have to outlast whatever tool I'm using this year. Steph Ango's phrase, and it's the single principle that decides my whole setup. If a note is trapped in a proprietary format or a hosted editor, I don't really own it, I'm renting it.

## The publishing pipeline this produced

Before I hand-built the current site I published straight out of Bear, see Figma and Bear are my daily tools. Bear's own WordPress publishing was too limited, and honestly I'd be happy never touching another WordPress site. I tried an Astro workflow with automated Bear exports on Netlify first, and it was too heavy and had too many moving parts for someone who isn't a developer. What worked was Blot, which turns any folder into a website, wired to iCloud.

The gap was frontmatter, since Bear exports don't have any. So I built an Apple Shortcut: it finds notes tagged draft, flips the tag to live, exports markdown to iCloud Drive, flattens nested tags, writes frontmatter with tags and modified date, and overwrites the file. Tagging a note in Bear was the publish button. The whole walkthrough is at /#writing/how-to-use-bear-as-a-cms.

## Why I moved off it

I wanted full control of the design, which is what lukevz.com is hand-built with vanilla HTML CSS and JS gave me. But nothing about the notes changed when I switched, which is the entire argument for file over app: the files just pointed somewhere new. Same reason 52 is local and markdown-based. I don't use Obsidian anymore either; I gave it over a year and the UI stayed clunky and the mobile experience frustrated me, and I take most of my notes on my iPhone. Hubs: PKM MOC, Site MOC.

Every year my wife and I pick a two-word theme and then review the year against it. The theme isn't a resolution, it's a lens: it decides which tradeoffs we say yes to for twelve months. 2024 was Consistency and Intentionality. 2025 was Remaking Possible. The review at the end is written publicly, which is the part that keeps me honest.

## How the review is structured

I review across the areas of a wheel of life rather than one big narrative: relationships, work, health, creativity, dwelling, travel, faith, and finance. Going area by area stops the loud parts of a year from swallowing the quiet ones. It's also where I notice the small habits that actually did the work, things like weekly check-ins and biweekly date nights, which look trivial written down and are the reason a hard year didn't break anything.

The theme is what makes it useful a year later. 2024's Consistency and Intentionality was about building the habits. 2025's Remaking Possible was about admitting some things weren't working and rebuilding them: I left PwC for Instinct, see PwC was an academy but I wanted to see my work land and I design software for veterinarians at Instinct, and we downsized from a four-bedroom house to a two-bedroom apartment. The lesson I carried out of it is that your nervous system matters more than your productivity, which is exactly what 2026 is built on in In 2026 I am building habits that regulate instead of optimize.

Both reviews are on the site in full: 2025 at /#writing/2025-year-in-review and 2024 at /#writing/2024--year-in-review. I fell into design systems around the summer of 2021, not by choice but by volume. I was a senior web designer at Blue Corona, a marketing agency, one of two seniors plus a few juniors, and we were responsible for a huge number of home-services website projects at once. There was no set size to a project: some sites ran hundreds of pages off a handful of custom templates. We had to start building reusable blocks or drown.

## The grayscale page generator

Figma was just getting popular and I helped move the team off Photoshop onto it. Then I helped build what was basically a web page generator: grayscale variations of every core marketing block, heroes, calls to action, forms, about sections, products and services, coupons, that you could drag into a file and swap out. That grew into a full system of buttons, icons, and hero lockups. Sites that used to take ten-plus hours of design time dropped to under two. I wrote about that in an old case study on automating workflows.

I was learning from Figma's free YouTube resources and Brad Frost's atomic design approach at the time. That agency grind is why I believe Design systems are a shared language not a component library: the components only mattered because the whole team used them the same way. It set up everything that came next at PwC; see I rebuilt PwC's design system in Figma to prove the switch. Hub: Design Systems MOC.

Document the points, not the maneuvers. I got this from watching Formula 1: the standings only record points, 25 for a win, 18 for second, and that clean tally is what survives the season. But the race itself is made of maneuvers, the overtakes, the pit calls, the tire management, the near misses. Those are what made it worth watching, and none of them show up in the table.

Gardening ideas works the same way. The maneuvers are the raw ingredients of my thinking: the articles I read, the notes I scribble, the conversations I'm reacting to. The points are the distilled insights I decide to keep, the published note, the idea worth carrying forward. You can try to capture every maneuver and you'll drown in it, and it still won't transmit the energy of being in the race. So I keep the points, credit the ingredients, and let the rest go.

This is the main reason my garden isn't a complete record of my thinking and I'm fine with that. It fits how I see the whole practice in A digital garden is a philosophy not a website, and it's why capture in Bear stays cheap and messy while what reaches the site is deliberate. I wrote this up at /#writing/documenting-points-vs-maneuvers. Hubs: PKM MOC, Site MOC.

TITLE: Six questions before touching any tools
TAGS: design, opinions, processes
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

Good design is an answer to a series of questions. Before anything else you need a crystal-clear understanding of the problem, and that's harder than it sounds. The more you try to define it, the more complex it feels. It's an uphill battle to figure out what the problem actually is, then to keep iterating until you can deliver the simplest version of a solution.

The six questions I always ask at the start:

- What problem are we solving?
- Who are we solving it for?
- Why are we solving it?
- Does it even need to be solved?
- Does it need to be solved now?
- Does it need to be solved by us?

I run these before touching any tools, right alongside Define the baseline first. The bar for the answer is Simple is the most elegant form of complexity. This is the core of my process at Design MOC.

TAGS: design, opinions
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

Design is mostly systematic pattern recognition, but the patterns that matter most aren't from other software. They're from the physical world. How do people know to push versus pull a door? How do they know where to park? Those patterns feel completely natural because they've been adopted at mass scale, and the best digital UX borrows from them, not from what another app does.

## Copying apps is templating, not pattern recognition

A lot of designers copy other software thinking they're doing pattern recognition. They're not. They're templating. Real pattern recognition means finding what's already familiar and natural to people in everyday life, then adapting it.

The caveat: people are complex and different. Some metaphors land for some users and completely miss others. Constantly reusing digital heuristics that work in some contexts won't always translate. You have to stay attuned to why something feels natural, not just that it does. This is the belief I'd defend hardest at Design MOC, and it's the same instinct behind Simple is the most elegant form of complexity.

What shocked me about designing for veterinarians is how much context switching and detail they hold while making genuinely hard calls in stressful situations. I knew being a vet was tough, but I had the happier notion that they mostly get to work with animals. Really they're seeing the heavy side of it, especially in the emergency clinics Instinct serves. That reframed a lot of my work at Instinct.

## One role can need three or four personas

The bigger surprise was that a single job title covers wildly different people. I was used to typecasting my users. At PwC I'd design for a CEO, a product manager, and an engineer, and those were clean, clear-cut roles. In veterinary medicine you can have three or four different types of doctors, CSRs (client service representatives), or vet techs under the same title, largely driven by the size of the practice and whether it's general practice or ER (emergency). So I almost need multiple personas for the same role. It's probably true in other industries too, but veterinary work is where it broke my old habit and forced me to run the Six questions before touching any tools harder. Hubs: Career MOC, Design MOC.

Design systems are my specialty, and my core take is that Design systems are a shared language not a component library. The components are the output; the real work is the decisions, the documentation, and adoption. I like design systems because they force you to think at the system level, which is where my head already lives; see I am wired for pattern recognition.

I didn't choose them so much as get forced into them: I fell into design systems by drowning in website volume at Blue Corona, the marketing agency where a reusable grayscale block system took sites from ten-plus hours down to under two. That experience became the pitch at PwC, the consulting firm where I spent 2022 through 2025: I rebuilt PwC's design system in Figma to prove the switch largely in my free time, then I pitched and led PwC's migration to Figma across 120-plus designers, then I ran the design system serving 3000 products at PwC as manager. What that rollout actually taught me is that Rolling out a design system is a teaching job: office hours and 40 pages of documentation moved adoption more than any component did. The scar tissue is real too: Figma variables v1 caused more harm than help at scale cost us months of cleanup and taught me not to bet a live library on a v1 platform feature.

Where I've landed after all of it: Design tokens are the unlock, for theming and now for how AI agents consume design, and Most companies do not need a custom design system. PwC justified custom; most teams should theme a popular base instead. Today the systems thinking continues at Instinct, where I design software for veterinarians at Instinct. 52 is a local markdown-based note-taking app I'm building. The idea is to stop outsourcing your thinking to AI and get back to that feeling of being in control you get with pen and paper: just focused on taking good notes again, one work week at a time.

## How it works

The core is a notes surface where you capture meetings and ideas. Those can be turned into action items, which automatically get tracked on a tasks page. You can tag collaborators and stakeholders, then filter by person to pull up everything about them quickly. Achievements and milestones can be turned into "epochs" so you can zoom out from the week-to-week and see your actual impact over time. It's also essentially a live CV: you're building the record as you go instead of scrambling to reconstruct it when you need to make a career move.

The philosophy behind it is the same as AI makes taste the differentiator: never outsource your thinking. It sits alongside the digital garden in how I work in public. Hub: PKM MOC.

SYNTHESIS across 18 notes

Design is a process of answering questions, and I prioritize defining the baseline and asking six core questions before touching any tools. My goal is to achieve simplicity, which I define as the most elegant form of complexity: a distilled solution that never sacrifices utility. I am wired for pattern recognition, and I believe the best patterns come from the physical world rather than other apps. Copying software is merely templating, not design.

My working style centers on removing layers between myself and the user, which is why I moved to Instinct to design veterinary software. I have learned that one role can require multiple personas, especially in complex environments like veterinary medicine. I also believe designers must think like business owners rather than order-takers, and I never get attached to my work. My taste is generally minimal, though I maintain a soft spot for skeuomorphism and Apple’s SF Pro font.

Regarding technology, AI amplifies your process but does not fix a broken one. Because AI makes execution easier, taste has become the primary differentiator. I use AI across my workflow to handle mechanical loads, allowing me to focus on judgment. While some tools can be built, I believe well-crafted software that brings joy is worth paying for.

SYNTHESIS across 16 notes

Design systems are my specialty, but I have learned that they are a shared language rather than a component library. The components are merely the output. The real work involves the decisions, the documentation, and the adoption process. I fell into this field at Blue Corona, where I built a grayscale block system that reduced design time from ten hours to under two. Later, at PwC, I rebuilt the design system in Figma, led a migration for 120 designers, and managed a system serving 3,000 products.

That experience taught me that rolling out a system is a teaching job. Documentation and office hours drive adoption far more than components do. I also learned to avoid betting a live library on a version one platform feature after Figma variables caused months of cleanup. Today, I am applying these lessons at Instinct, where I design software for veterinarians. My current approach starts with tokens, which provide the foundation for theming. Most companies do not need a custom system and should instead theme a popular base like Tailwind or shadcn/ui. This is especially relevant now because AI agents can easily consume design tokens and standard bases. Ultimately, a design system succeeds or fails based on shared understanding, not on the number of components shipped.

SYNTHESIS across 5 notes

My journey with Figma began around the summer of 2021 at Blue Corona, where the sheer volume of web projects forced me to abandon Photoshop for a more efficient, component-based workflow. By early 2022, I leveraged that experience to pitch and lead the migration from Sketch, Abstract, and InVision to Figma at PricewaterhouseCoopers. I rebuilt their entire design system from scratch, taking on most of the work myself to prove the platform's value. This effort eventually scaled to support 120 designers and 3000 products.

I learned the hard way that rolling out a design system is primarily a teaching job. Beyond building the library, I upskilled the entire department through extensive documentation and office hours. However, my experience with Figma variables in 2023 serves as a cautionary tale. While I genuinely needed the feature for theme switching, the v1 implementation caused months of chaos across our library due to cache versioning and corrupted instances. As of July 2026, my settled position is that a v1 platform feature is never mature enough to bet a live library on when the blast radius includes hundreds of downstream files. Despite those struggles, Figma remains my primary design tool, and I still believe that design tokens are the ultimate unlock for scaling systems.

My perspective on artificial intelligence is rooted in the idea that these tools are accelerators rather than solutions for broken processes. If your process is solid, you gain efficiency, but if it is flawed, artificial intelligence only accelerates those failures. My work on Software Development Lifecycle Canvas at PricewaterhouseCoopers taught me that fundamentals like the Six questions remain critical.

Because artificial intelligence can execute tasks for almost anyone, taste and judgment have become the primary differentiators. You must never outsource your thinking. This belief extends to my technical choices, such as using design tokens. Tokens provide the necessary context for agents to understand design systems, which is why building on established bases like Material, shadcn/ui, or Tailwind is often more effective than creating something bespoke.

I integrate artificial intelligence across my entire workflow to handle mechanical loads. I use Wispr Flow for dictation, Granola or Gemini for meeting transcripts, Cursor and Claude Code for rapid prototyping, and Notion Artificial Intelligence for organization. By offloading these tasks, I can focus on judgment and craft. While some suggest building every tool yourself, I believe well-built software that brings joy is worth paying for. Tools like MyMind, Granola, and Bear provide a level of quality and trust that remains valuable even in an era of rapid automation.

When it comes to specific preferences, I am a huge proponent of pineapple on pizza, and Hawaiian pizza is often my go-to order.

My beverage habits are seasonal and specific. I am currently on a cold brew kick, which is my preferred non-alcoholic choice, especially during the summer in Atlanta. When winter arrives, I switch back to hot coffee. I consider myself a nice-coffee person, so I frequent recommended coffee shops in Atlanta and pull my own shots on an espresso machine at home. If I am at a bar, my go-to order is a good margarita or a golden or amber ale. These habits reflect my settled perspective on dining and drinking as of the summer of 2026.

In 2026, my focus has shifted toward building habits that regulate my nervous system rather than simply optimizing my productivity. I am prioritizing a calmer mind and a more regulated environment, moving away from multitasking toward being present in the moment. This approach is reflected in my daily routines, such as morning pages, consistent movement, and analog activities like scrapbooking.

Professionally, I am currently a senior product designer at Instinct, the veterinary software company. My work there is centered on reducing the stress of overworked veterinarians, which aligns with my broader belief in removing layers between myself and the user. I am approaching our design system work with a tokens-first mindset, applying the hard-won lessons from my time at PricewaterhouseCoopers. While I previously managed a massive system for thousands of products there, my current challenge is scaling these principles effectively at a smaller company. I have learned that platform features like Figma variables require caution, as a version one release can cause significant instability at scale. Ultimately, I remain convinced that design systems are a shared language, not just a component library, and that design tokens are the essential unlock for modern workflows.

In 2025, my focus centered on the principle of file over app. I keep everything in plain markdown files because my notes must outlast any specific tool. If a note is trapped in a proprietary format, I am merely renting it. This philosophy led me to build a publishing pipeline using Bear and Blot, allowing me to own my content while maintaining a hand-built site. I stopped using Obsidian because the mobile experience frustrated me, and I take most of my notes on my iPhone.

My annual review for 2025 was themed Remaking Possible. This lens helped me admit when things were not working, leading me to leave PricewaterhouseCoopers for Instinct, the veterinary software company, and to downsize my living space. I learned that my nervous system matters more than my productivity, which informs my 2026 goal of building habits that regulate rather than optimize.

I also clarified how I document my work. I distinguish between points and maneuvers, a concept I borrowed from Formula 1. Maneuvers are the raw ingredients of thinking, while points are the distilled insights worth keeping. I publish only the points to avoid drowning in the process. Ultimately, digital gardening allows me to escape the self-promotion of social media and return to a space of messy, low-stakes exploration.
